$comment: The authored-city contract — docs/authored-city.md, all six items. citycheck.mjs asserts against this. Five of the six read the generator's PLACEMENT DATA rather than pixels, because they are checks on the decisions and not on the render; the saturation reserve is the exception and says so. Written before the generator existed, so that the gate could fail before there was anything to pass it.

region.$comment: The square of chunks the placement assertions are computed over, in chunk coordinates inclusive. 10x10 at 128 m is 1280 m square — large enough that a coefficient of variation means something and small enough to serialise.

clumping.$comment: docs/authored-city.md §1. Coefficient of variation of prop density across chunks. Grid-with-jitter gives a CV near 0.1; low-frequency noise with placement inside it gives well over 1. The floor is at 0.6 because that is where the two are unambiguously different — a city at 0.5 is a city somebody smoothed.
clumping.$minPopulatedChunks: A CV can also be made large by leaving almost everything empty, which is the degenerate way to pass this. At least this fraction of chunks must have content in them.

$SESSION_NOTE: The `sceneWalk` and `pedestrians` blocks below are checks on content that does not exist yet, or on a comparison nothing has ever made. Both are RED today and are supposed to be. They are written before the thing they measure because a check written afterwards is a check fitted to it — and because CONTRACT §0 rule 5 forbids ever loosening one.

sceneWalk.$comment: docs/authored-city.md has no item for this and it is not one of the six. It is here because of HOW the other five are measured: they read the generator's placement data, which is the right source for a claim about the generator and the wrong source for a claim about the city. A GATE THAT READS CONFIG VERIFIES THE CONFIG.
sceneWalk.$derivation: SESSION 5's viaduct. `pierEvery: 34` was written in the landmark data and `i % 3 === 0` was written in the code, and what shipped was a pier every 48 m. Every gate passed. Nothing anywhere compared the number that was written down against the number that was built, because every gate was reading the same side of that comparison. This walks the live scene instead — `instanceMatrix.count` off each InstancedMesh, plus the per-kind breakdown each mesh recorded as it was assembled — and requires the two to agree.
sceneWalk.$WHY_IT_IS_RED_TODAY: The merge that took the detail ring from nine draw calls a chunk to five put buildings, crowns, props and road patches into one InstancedMesh, so until this session the scene had no way to say how many props it drew. The label exists now; what does not exist is a delivered census matching a declared one for the props, because the props are placed without a collision test against the buildings (src/lib/citygen.js — the scatter over `island` tests keep-outs and landmarks and not the perimeter ring it sits inside). That fix is 4b's. Until then this reports the gap rather than hiding it.
sceneWalk.$maxUnderdrawnFraction: An InstancedMesh may draw fewer instances than it allocated — three keeps `count` and `instanceMatrix.count` separate. A pool that allocated 700 and draws 40 is a different fact from one that allocated 40, and for a particle layer it is the whole fact. Above this fraction of meshes, the scene is carrying instance buffers it is not using.
sceneWalk.$maxPropsInsideBuildings: Props whose centre lies inside a building's footprint. Zero, and it is zero today at 0 because nothing measures it — see requirePropCollisionTest.
sceneWalk.$signage: SESSION 14. TWO ASSERTIONS AND THEY ARE THE CONTRACT §7.2 PAIR. `minSignMountings` counts the generator's vocabulary; `minSignStandoffSpreadM` measures the property that vocabulary was assumed to carry, off the DELIVERED instance matrices. Session 3 shipped one mounting and a colour roll, and a flat sign on a wall is edge-on to anyone walking down the street — the same sentence `block.js` has carried in a comment since session 3 without the generated city ever acting on it.
sceneWalk.$maxSignsInsideBuildings: ZERO, AND IT WAS 208 OF 208. `citygen` writes a sign's position as its BUILDING'S CENTRE and `city.js` offset that by 0.5 m along the outward normal and called it the wall. A building is 15 to 26 m deep, so 0.5 m from its centre is 7 to 12 m inside it: measured over the 49 chunks round the origin at seed 1337, straight out of the pure generator, ALL 208 signs sat inside their own building at a median depth of 9.51 m, minimum 7.05, maximum 12.43. Not one of the streamed city's 408 sign quads has ever reached a frame. This is CONTRACT §9's table with a building's centre used as its elevation, and it is measured from the delivered matrices because the placement data holds the centre and has no opinion about it (§9.1: a gate that reads config verifies the config).
sceneWalk.$minSignMountings: 4: flush, projecting, roof, freestanding. A COUNT OF CATEGORIES AND NOTHING MORE, which is why it is paired. Delivered over the budget's own region at seed 1337: flush 75, projecting 64, roof 46, freestanding 23 of 208.
sceneWalk.$minSignStandoffSpreadM: 1.0 m, DERIVED FROM BOTH DIRECTIONS. The metric is p90 - p10 of the 3-D distance from each delivered sign quad to the nearest building box. THE NEGATIVE CONTROL IS EXACT: a flush-only city — which is what session 3 shipped and what session 14 found buried — puts every quad at the same 0.12 m fascia standoff and reads a spread of EXACTLY 0.000, by construction rather than by calibration, which is the property `darkFraction` did not have (CONTRACT §7.3). Delivered at seed 1337: p10 0.120 m, p90 2.504 m, spread 2.384 m over 604 quads, so the floor sits 2.4x under the delivered value. 1.0 rather than something smaller because the spread has to mean a POPULATION and not an exception: p90 - p10 exceeds 1.0 only if at least a tenth of the quads stand a metre or more off their elevation, and one narrow blade among two hundred fascias is not a mounting vocabulary. Delivered, 220 of 604 quads (36%) stand 0.8 m or further out.

pedestrians.$comment: docs/authored-city.md §1 asks for clumping and measures it on props. Pedestrians are the same claim about a different population and they cannot borrow the props' number: a bollard is placed where the density field is high, a person is where the density field is high AND there is somewhere to be going.
pedestrians.$derivation: THE FLOOR IS THE PROPS' MEASURED CV, NOT A NEW GUESS. Grid-with-jitter measures a coefficient of variation near 0.1; the low-frequency density field this generator uses measures 0.302 raw and 0.712 once the placement takes its cube (city-budget.json → clumping, and the delivered figure is 0.712). Pedestrians follow that same field AND a destination term, so their CV must EXCEED the props' or the destination term is doing nothing — a crowd no more clumped than the bollards is bollards that walk. 0.7 is the props' delivered 0.712 rounded down, which makes the floor a measurement rather than a preference. If 4b finds it unreachable, the objection CONTRACT §0 rule 5 accepts is an impossibility proof carrying arithmetic, and the arithmetic to beat is this one.
pedestrians.$minPopulatedFraction: The degenerate way to get a high CV is to leave almost everything empty. Lower than the props' 0.55 because a city has streets with nobody on them and blocks with nobody in them, and both are correct.
pedestrians.$minTotal: A CV over three people is a CV over three people.
pedestrians.$requireEmptyChunksDeclared: SESSION 4b, AND IT IS A HOLE IN THE 4a INSTRUMENT RATHER THAN NEW POLICY. `harness.pedestrianCensus` builds its per-chunk map ONLY from objects carrying `userData.noctisPedestrians`, so a chunk with nobody in it that declares nothing does not appear at all: the mean is then taken over occupied chunks only, the CV collapses toward the within-occupied spread, and `populated` — counts.filter(c > 0) — goes to 1.0 and clears the 0.35 floor for free. Both bounds would have been passed by the shape of the reporting rather than by the crowd. Every chunk in the simulated ring declares, including `count: 0`.
pedestrians.$derivation_straightness: DESTINATIONS RATHER THAN RANDOM WALKS, AS A NUMBER. Straightness is |net displacement| / (path length) per pedestrian over a fixed window, averaged over the population. For an isotropic random walk of step length l and N steps, E|net| is the Rayleigh mean l*sqrt(pi*N/4), so straightness = sqrt(pi/(4N)) = 0.886/sqrt(N) and depends only on how many decorrelations fit in the window. Over a 20 s window at 1.4 m/s the path is 28 m, and across the whole plausible band of decorrelation times a random walk gives: tau 0.5 s -> N 40 -> 0.140; tau 1.5 s -> N 13.3 -> 0.243; tau 3 s -> N 6.7 -> 0.343. A destination-driven walker on a 128 m street lattice turns corners: a straight leg is 1.0, one right-angle turn is 0.707, two is about 0.6, and standing still at a destination changes NEITHER numerator nor denominator so dwell does not enter. THE FLOOR IS 0.55 — above the entire random-walk band including its laziest end, below one-corner-per-window. It is the same shape of argument as the CV floor: not 'is it clumped' but 'is it more clumped than the thing that already exists', here 'is it straighter than the thing that has no destination'.
pedestrians.$minArrivalsPerMinute: A destination nobody reaches is a heading. Arrivals per pedestrian per minute: a 45 m mean trip at 1.4 m/s is 32 s plus a 6 s dwell, so 1.58 per minute is the expectation. The floor is at a third of it, which fails a system where most pedestrians are still walking toward their first destination when the window closes.

streetLevel.$comment: SESSION 4b. Shops, stalls and food stands at street level, against the allowance 4a left in the light pool. Counted off the live scene by `sceneCensus`, never off the generator's description.
streetLevel.$derivation_count: A PITCH DEPENDS ON FOOTFALL, AND FOOTFALL IS THE DENSITY FIELD ITSELF RATHER THAN ITS CUBE. Buildings use `0.12 + 0.88*density^2.2` and props use `density^3`, both of which are deliberately harsh so that most chunks are empty and a few are dense. A stallholder is different in kind: below some number of passers-by a pitch is not worth setting up and above it one more stall is marginal, which is a threshold and not a power law. So stalls use `round(30 * smoothstep(0.34, 0.85, density))` — zero below CITY.lowDetailThreshold, saturating at 30 per chunk. The lower knee is the generator's own dead-zone threshold rather than a second number. At the field's mean density near 0.5 that is 7 per chunk, and over the 25 chunks of the near ring (road surface and street lamps exist only for ring <= 2) about 175. Kerb length per chunk is 2 owned edges x 128 m x 2 sides = 512 m, so 7 stalls is one per 73 m of kerb on an average block and one per 17 m on a dense one.
streetLevel.$minStallKinds: Three: an infill pitch in a shut shop bay, a free-standing market stall, and a food stand. Different silhouettes and different reasons to exist, which is what stops a row of them reading as one repeated object.
streetLevel.$minStallKinds_s14: RAISED FROM 3 TO 5 AGAINST THE DELIVERED WORLD, which is what a ratchet is for. Session 14 added `produce` — a pitched awning, a raked two-tier display and crates, where the other three are flat canopies over a level table — and `rack`, a hanging rail against a shut bay where `infill` is a trestle. Delivered over the near ring at seed 1337: market 157, produce 111, food 51, infill 14, rack 8, total 341 pitches with 1 abandoned. AND THIS FLOOR WAS NEVER READ BY ANY GATE UNTIL SESSION 14 — see `$UNREAD_UNTIL_S14`.
streetLevel.$UNREAD_UNTIL_S14: EVERY THRESHOLD IN THIS BLOCK WAS WRITTEN IN SESSION 4b AND NO GATE READ ONE OF THEM UNTIL SESSION 14. `minStallsNearRing`, `minStallKinds`, `maxStallLightSlots` and the whole `$derivation_count` paragraph sat here being cited and never evaluated: CONTRACT §9.1's 'a value written in config that the code does not read', with a block instead of a pier spacing, and it is worse than the pier was because a reader opening this file finds derivations that read as guarantees. `citycheck` now reads all of them off `harness.stallCensus()`, which is the LIVE module's own count rather than the generator's description.
streetLevel.$awnings: THE §7.2 PAIR. `minAwningCloths` counts the vocabulary; `minAwningChromaSpreadLinear` measures the property that vocabulary was assumed to carry. Session 13 shipped ONE canopy reflectance — [0.3, 0.288, 0.262] — on every stall of every kind in the city, and a count of kinds could not see it because the kinds were three and the colour was one.
streetLevel.$minAwningCloths: 8. Delivered 8 of 8, because the cloth is rolled per pitch over 341 pitches and every entry turns up. These are LINEAR reflectances of dyed canvas and PVC, not authored sRGB tones: a saturated awning is 0.30 to 0.45 in its own channel and 0.04 to 0.12 in the others, because dyed cloth is a subtractive filter over a white weave and cannot be both saturated and bright. Two of the eight are neutrals — unbleached canvas and a grey tarpaulin — because that is what most of a real market is.
streetLevel.$minAwningChromaSpreadLinear: 0.30. The measurement is the WIDEST Euclidean separation between two delivered cloth reflectances in linear RGB. THE NEGATIVE CONTROL IS EXACT AND IT IS WHAT SHIPPED: one colour on every canopy reads 0.0000 by construction rather than by calibration, which is the property `darkFraction` did not have (CONTRACT §7.3). Delivered: the red [0.36, 0.085, 0.070] against the blue [0.055, 0.130, 0.330] is hypot(0.305, -0.045, -0.260) = 0.402, so the floor sits 1.34x under the delivered value. 0.30 rather than 0.40 because a spread is a claim about a POPULATION and the population is rolled per pitch: a route that happened to draw seven of the eight must still pass, and the widest pair among any seven of these eight is at least 0.31.
streetLevel.$maxStallLightSlots: THE SAME ARITHMETIC THAT GAVE TAIL LIGHTS ZERO SLOTS, APPLIED HONESTLY RATHER THAN AS A SLOGAN. A tail lamp gets none because 0.5 lux at 11 m is 3% of a carriageway held at 16 lux: it is not illuminating anything. A food stand's griddle and worklight are the opposite case — about 400 lm into a 2 m hemisphere is 32 lux on the stallholder and the counter at 1 m, twice the ambient, and an emissive plane cannot light the person standing behind it because nothing in this project treats emissive geometry as a light source (CONTRACT §5.6: an unpatched material is not lit by local lights, and a patched one is not lit BY an emitter). So food stands get a slot each and nothing else does. 12 is the ceiling: the pool's margin after 52 block + 196 lamp + 96 traffic is 40, and spending 12 of it leaves 28 for whatever session 5 wants. The claim this makes is falsifiable — if a stall's own lit surfaces read as lighting the street, the slot was not needed.
streetLevel.$requireStallsMostlyEmissive: Fraction of stall fixtures that carry NO light slot. A market stall's strip light, a canopy edge, a menu board and a shop-bay infill are all emissive geometry. Only the food stand's worklight earns a slot, and there are far fewer food stands than stalls.

vintage.$maxDeadSignageFraction: A dead sign is wear; a city of dead signs is a blackout. The upper bound is not in the addendum and is added here because a floor with no ceiling is passed most easily by going all the way.

alignment.$comment: §3. Both bounds matter and the addendum says so: large randomness looks broken, small consistent deviation looks real.
alignment.$minDeviationDeg: An object 0.001 degrees off axis is on the axis. Below this it does not count as deviating, which is what stops the fraction from being met by numerical dust.

saturation.$comment: §4, and the one criterion here that is measured in pixels rather than in placement data. Sampled along the night route so it is the whole route and not one lucky frame.
saturation.$SPECIFICATION_CORRECTION: docs/authored-city.md §4 says 'no more than 12% of screen pixels above 0.6 saturation'. Measured literally, the night route delivers 90.9% mean and 100% peak — and NO correct frame can do better. THE ARITHMETIC: a high-pressure sodium lamp's chromaticity, normalised to luminance 1, is (1.0, 0.42, 0.06) (lib/color.js, EMITTER_CHROMA.sodium). HSV saturation is (max-min)/max, which is scale-invariant, so ANY surface whose illumination is dominated by street lighting measures 1 - 0.06/1.0 = 0.94 regardless of how dark it is. A night street lit by HPS is therefore ~94% saturated over its entire lit area as a matter of physics, before a single sign is placed. A perfect result — an HPS-lit street with no signage at all — still measures about 90%, which is 7.5x the ceiling. The threshold is unreachable by any physically correct frame, which is the one objection CONTRACT allows, and this is its arithmetic.
saturation.$WHY_THIS_IS_A_CORRECTION_AND_NOT_A_RELA: The addendum's own prose, two lines above the check, says a real neon street 'is mostly sodium orange, dead beige concrete, dirty white fluorescent... and THEN a few saturated signs that pop precisely because everything around them is drab'. Sodium orange is 0.94 saturation. So the check as literally written forbids the thing the text immediately above it asks for, and it is the check that is wrong about what it was measuring — the STATE.md test for a specification correction rather than a threshold reduction. What the addendum wants reserved is GLOW: chromatic things bright enough to compete for attention. A dark orange road surface is chromatic and does not glow.
saturation.$WHAT_CHANGED: The 12% and the 0.6 are the addendum's numbers and are unchanged. A pixel now has to be saturated AND bright to count, which is what 'if the whole frame glows, nothing glows' means. Nothing else in this file moved.
saturation.$valueThreshold: HSV value, on the encoded frame. 0.5 is the midpoint: a sign face, a lit window and a lamp bowl clear it; a sodium-lit road surface, a lit wall and the sky glow do not. That is precisely the line between the signage the reserve is protecting and the drab surround that gives it its impact.
saturation.$estimator: THE MEDIAN OF THE PER-RUN MAXIMA, OVER `runs` FRESH PAGE LOADS. CONTRACT §0 rule 6, applied to the last gate in this project that decided a threshold from a single draw. WHAT WAS WRONG: `satMax` is the maximum over 12 frames of one route, an extreme-value statistic dominated by whichever bloom halo happened to be nearest the lens, and session 5 measured it at 10.15 / 10.19 / 11.10 percent across three separate invocations — a run-to-run spread of 0.95 points against a margin of 0.90 at the worst draw. That is the `downtown_dense` incident with a percentage instead of a percentile. THE SAMPLE POSITIONS ARE DETERMINISTIC (`sampleRouteAt` at fixed parameters), so the spread is not sampling noise in the route: it is what differs between two loads of the same page — which chunks had streamed, what the TAA history had converged to, where the rain was. A RUN IS THEREFORE A FRESH PAGE LOAD; twelve more samples off the page already open would pool over the one thing that is already deterministic. THE MEDIAN OF PER-RUN MAXIMA AND NOT THE MAXIMUM OVER POOLED FRAMES, and that is the whole reason this is written down: the 12% ceiling was derived against the max over TWELVE samples, and the max over 36 pooled samples is a DIFFERENT QUANTITY — stochastically larger by construction, growing with the number of runs — so comparing it to this ceiling would be §9 with a statistic instead of a length. NOT THE MEAN, for `capture.$estimator`s reason: the median of three discards exactly one contaminated observation and 10.15 / 10.19 / 11.10 is two agreeing draws and one high one. NO THRESHOLD MOVED: `maxFraction` is 0.12 before and after and `minFraction` is 0.004 before and after. WHAT POOLING THEN MEASURED, AND IT IS WORSE THAN THE PROBLEM IT WAS WRITTEN FOR. Six per-run maxima across two invocations of this gate, every run with 25 of 25 field bakes landed and 25 chunks resident: 8.64 / 9.68 / 9.78 / 11.48 / 11.74 / 11.74 percent. THE SPREAD IS 3.10 POINTS, not the 0.95 session 5 recorded — those three invocations were a tight draw from a wide distribution, and reading a noise floor off three samples of an extreme-value statistic is the same mistake one level down. The two POOLED medians were 9.68 and 11.74, so the estimator`s own reproducibility is 2.06 points while the margin at the higher of them is 0.26. THE RESERVE IS THEREFORE ON THE LINE AND THE POOLING IS WHAT SHOWED IT: the single draw was not merely noisy, it was hiding that this content sits at its ceiling. Raising `runs` does not rescue it — the median of n has standard error about 1.54/sqrt(n) points here, so 0.26 points of margin would need about 35 runs — and the ceiling may not move (§0 rule 5). The honest report is that this gate is green by less than its own resolution, exactly as `night_rain` is against its frame-time ceiling, and the next session that spends saturation has no margin to spend. ONE MORE THING THAT COST A MEASUREMENT: the first version of the multi-run loop reloaded the page and sampled without waiting for the city, and returned 10.93 / 6.82 / 9.03 — `sampleRouteAt` settles 30 frames, which moves the camera on an already-streamed city and does not build one. Every run now runs `waitForCity` and the printed line reports each run`s bakes, so a half-lit run cannot be pooled in as though it were a second sample of the same quantity. FIVE TWO-SIDED FALSIFYING CASES live beside the estimator in citycheck.mjs — one high run of three must not fail, three over must, two of three over must, exactly at the ceiling must not, and a dead reserve must still fail the FLOOR, because a pooled estimator that rescued only one direction would be a rubber stamp with an error bar.
saturation.$runs: 3, WHICH IS `capture.runs` FROM budget.json AND DELIBERATELY THE SAME NUMBER. The median of three is the smallest pool that can discard a contaminated observation at all, and a different count here would be a second thing to derive for no reason. The cost is two extra page loads and 24 extra screenshots at 1280x720. `--satruns=1` overrides it for a fast look, and the printed line says how many runs it pooled so a number taken that way cannot be mistaken for the gate`s.
saturation.$minFraction: The reserve is a reserve, not a ban. A night city with no saturated pixels at all has thrown away the thing the reserve exists to protect.
saturation.$minBrightFraction: SESSION 16. THE FLOOR THAT PAIRS WITH THE CEILING, AND IT READS THE OTHER HALF OF THE CEILING'S OWN PREDICATE. `glows` is a CONJUNCTION — saturation > 0.6 AND value > 0.5 — so there are two ways to lower it and the reserve is only asking for one. Desaturating moves the chromaticity and leaves `max(r,g,b)` alone; darkening pushes the pixel under the value threshold and takes it out of the numerator for the wrong reason. Every reduction this project made in answer to a saturation red was of the second kind: POST.glareStrength 0.15 → 0.075 (constants.js:215-240, swept explicitly against this ceiling: 0.15 → 15.3%, 0.11 → 13.0%, 0.09 → 11.8%, 0.075 → 10.9%), LIGHT.signPlateNits 6500 → 86 (constants.js:44-77, in the run that found the reserve red at 12.49%), NITS_TAIL/BRAKE/FRONT 555/2220/4400 → 45/180/70 (traffic.js:1444-1503, after a 16.01% peak), and the 2.78 m marker line built, measured and declined (traffic.js:1097-1111). Each is defensible alone; the SUM of them had no instrument, because the only thing watching was a ceiling that a darker frame satisfies by construction. CONTRACT §7.2 is normally a category count paired with a property measurement; this is the same rule one step in — a bound on a conjunction paired with a bound on the conjunct that was doing the work.
saturation.$minBrightFraction_number: 0.06, DERIVED, AND THE DERIVATION SAYS WHAT IT DOES NOT KNOW. Delivered on the night_rain route, three runs x 12 samples: per-run means 8.36 / 7.99 / 8.39 percent, pooled 8.36 (median of per-run means), observed run-to-run RANGE 0.40 points. The floor is 7.99 − 6.0 = 1.99 points under the WORST run, which is 5.0x that range — §0 rule 6's requirement on any threshold over a drifting quantity, and the multiple is stated rather than assumed because this quantity is not a count. WHAT IT IS NOT: it is not derived from what a night city OUGHT to have above half-code. Nobody has computed that, and dressing the number up as though somebody had is the thing §9 rule 5 forbids. What makes it a ratchet rather than a guess is what makes `floors.visibleInstances` one — it sits under today's delivered value, it is measured on the delivered artefact rather than on placement data, and it may only ever go up. The next session can disagree with the arithmetic; it cannot disagree with the taste, because there is none in it.
saturation.$minBrightFraction_estimator: THE MEDIAN OF THE PER-RUN MEANS, AND IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT THE CEILING'S ESTIMATOR MIRRORED. The ceiling pools the per-run MAXIMUM because 'does anywhere glow too much' is convicted by one frame and its failure is local — a bloom halo, a hauler at the lens. 'The city has gone dark' is a shift of the whole distribution, and a per-run MINIMUM over twelve samples would be set by whichever sample faced a wall or a bridge soffit: an extreme-value statistic on the dark side, which is exactly the defect `$estimator` was written to take OUT of the ceiling. Mirroring would have been tidy and would have measured a different quantity, which is CONTRACT §9's failure mode with a statistic instead of a length. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, and it is the reason to record this: in the same three runs the ceiling's estimator spread 4.75 points (per-run maxima 10.20 / 14.79 / 10.04) and the floor's spread 0.40 points (8.36 / 7.99 / 8.39). The floor is 11.9x the more repeatable of the two, on the same pixels of the same frames of the same route — so the pair is not symmetric in what it can resolve, and the ceiling remains the one that cannot decide a 1-point margin.
saturation.$minBrightFraction_controls: CONTRACT §7.3, and the controls are in citycheck.mjs beside the metric, run by `--falsify`. A 70 x 10 frame built from a repeating 10-pixel period, sampled at the gate's own stride of 7 — coprime to 10, so the 100 samples hit each residue class exactly ten times and the sampled proportions ARE the period's. Hand-computed before any run: base glow 20% / bright 50%; x1.25 gives 70% / 100% (BOTH RISE); x0.60 gives 0% / 0% (BOTH FALL — the ratchet performed on purpose, ceiling satisfied and floor breached); desaturate gives 0% / 50% (glow falls, bright EXACTLY unchanged, because each channel moves toward the pixel's own max and that max is a fixed point of the transform). All four matched to the digit on the first run. The third is the one that makes this a pair rather than two floors: without it a reader could believe `bright` is `glows` again with a looser threshold, and the invariance is the proof that it is a different quantity. The subset relation glows ⊆ bright is asserted on every control, and the budget sanity block refuses a `minBrightFraction` at or under `minFraction` for the same reason — a floor implied by another floor can never fire, which is §7.1's quiet gate.
saturation.$SESSION_4b_ALLOCATION: THE RESERVE HAD 1.52 POINTS LEFT BEFORE THIS SESSION ADDED A SINGLE LIT THING — 10.48% peak against 12% — and three new populations want a share of it. The ceiling is not moved; the share is derived and then measured. PEDESTRIANS: silhouette area is the integral over the frustum of (0.6 * 1.70 * 0.45 m^2) / (d^2 * theta^2) against 0.06 people per m^2 of pavement over a pavement area fraction of 0.13125, which is 11 931 * ln(d_max/d_min) px^2; from 3 m to 120 m that is 44 013 px^2 = 1.194% of the frame. Cap the saturated share at one pedestrian in five wearing one chromatic garment covering the torso (about 35% of a standing silhouette), so 0.20 * 0.35 = 7.0% of pedestrian pixels, i.e. 0.084 points. VEHICLES: a full-width rear light line is 1.8 x 0.06 = 0.108 m^2, which is 257 500/d^2 px^2; ten receding vehicles at an 18.4 m spacing from 10 m sum to 3210 px^2 = 0.087 points, and tripling it for the bloom halo and the SSR reflection in the wet road gives 0.26. STALLS: budgeted at 0.45, the largest share of the three, because a canopy edge and a menu board are large chromatic surfaces at close range. TOTAL 0.79 of the 1.52, leaving 0.73. THE RISK IS REAL AND IS NAMED: the current 10.48% peak is dominated by ONE streetlamp's bloom halo close to the lens, so the peak sample is fragile in both directions — new geometry that OCCLUDES that halo lowers it. Measured either way in STATE.md rather than predicted.
saturation.$SESSION_4b_COLOUR_DISCIPLINE: city.js SIGN_CHROMA is 'six and no more' because the reserve is spent by the NUMBER of different saturated things, not by their brightness. Vehicle and stall lighting reuse that palette and add no seventh chromaticity; headlamps are cool white, which has near-zero HSV saturation and cannot enter this measurement at all.

falsify.$comment: CONTRACT §7. Every assertion in this gate has a known case that makes it fail, and `node tools/citycheck.mjs --falsify` exercises every one. `gateaudit` runs it as a subprocess and fails if any declared assertion id is uncovered. See tools/budget.json -> falsify for why this became a rule: three gates in this project went quiet rather than red, and a quiet gate is indistinguishable from a green one in every report.

negativeSpace.$comment: §5. Parking, empty lot, industrial yard, park. Emptiness is what makes density feel dense.

river.$comment: SESSION 15. The river, and the two assertions are the CONTRACT §7.2 PAIR. `minBridgeStructures` counts the generator's vocabulary; `minBridgeAboveDeckSpreadM` measures the property that vocabulary was assumed to carry, off the DELIVERED boxes. A count of three structures that are all flat decks is exactly the failure `trafficLights.minBodyTypes: 4` had when it passed at 5 on five flat-topped grey boxes.
river.$minBridgeStructures: THREE, AND IT IS GUARANTEED BY CONSTRUCTION RATHER THAN BY LUCK. Drawing a crossing's era from `CITY_ERAS`' own weights gives P(arch) 0.42, P(girder) 0.49, P(cable) 0.09, so the three crossings inside this file's own region would deliver all three about one seed in nine. `bridgeStructure` therefore deals a seeded PERMUTATION of the three per group of three crossings — a city builds a bridge at most once a generation and does not replace one with a copy of its neighbour — so any complete group carries one of each. Delivered at seed 1337 over crossings i=-1..1 (x = -512, 0, 512): arch, girder, cable. COUNTED OVER THE REGION'S OWN CROSSINGS THROUGH THE PURE GENERATOR AND NOT OVER THE BUILT WINDOW, which is CONTRACT §7.2's own split: a category floor is a statement about the generator's vocabulary, and `river.js` builds a 1024 m window while the crossings are 512 m apart, so counting the built window would make this floor a statement about where the gate's camera happened to stand. The PAIRED measurement below is read off what was actually built.
river.$minBridgeAboveDeckSpreadM: THE PAIRED MEASUREMENT, AND IT IS THE SILHOUETTE ABOVE THE DECK LINE because that is the only part of a bridge that reads from half a kilometre. A steel plate girder puts every millimetre of its structure UNDER the deck and shows nothing above it but a 1.05 m parapet; a bowstring arch rises span/6, which on a 114 m channel is 19.0 m; a cable-stayed tower rises 0.28 of the span, 29.4 m. Delivered spread at seed 1337: 29.38 - 1.05 = 28.33 m. The floor is 12 m, which is the smallest spread that could not be produced by three decks differing only in parapet height (the tallest parapet anybody builds is about 1.4 m, so three flat decks span at most 0.5 m) and is comfortably under a spread that any two of the three structures already deliver.
river.$minBridgesBuilt: A crossing every `RIVER.bridgeEvery * chunkSize` = 512 m, and the module builds `CITY.detailRadius * chunkSize` = 512 m either side of the camera, so the built window is 1024 m and holds two or three crossings depending on where the camera stands. The floor is 2. Zero would mean the bridge builder never ran, which is the state in which the walkability flood fill fails and this floor tells you WHY before the flood fill tells you THAT.
river.$minLandmarkClearanceM: ANYTHING PLACED PROCEDURALLY IS TESTED AGAINST THE EXISTING OCCUPANCY (CONTRACT §9.1), AND AN AUTHORED PLACEMENT IS NOT EXEMPT. The river's course is authored in `citygen.js` and the paragraph above it claims 11.2 m of clearance from the condenser's AABB and 11.4 m from the stack's; this is the assertion that makes the claim checkable. Measured by walking every landmark's AABB in x at 1 m and taking the smallest gap between the water's two edges and the box. Delivered at seed 1337: 21.16 m, on the stack. The floor is 8 m — under the delivered figure by a factor of 2.6 and over zero by enough that a future change to the meander cannot put water through masonry without saying so.
river.$minLandmarksAcrossWater: ORIENTATION, ASKED FROM THE PAVEMENT RATHER THAN FROM 200 M UP. `landmarks.minVisibleFromElevation` is the establishing shot and it is already 8 of 8; this is the shot the river exists for. Two eyes at 1.74 m, one on each bank at x = 64 (a station between crossings, so neither is standing on a bridge looking down it), each counting the landmarks on the FAR side of the water. From the south bank that can only be the condenser, which is the one landmark the river separates from the city; from the north bank it is whatever of the seven southern ones the far frontage leaves visible. THE FLOOR IS 3 and it is a floor on the PAIR: one sighting would be satisfied by the condenser alone, which is a fact about where the condenser stands rather than about the river being open. Delivered at seed 1337: see the run.

landmarks.$comment: §6. The item that does the most work for the least effort. Hand-placed, not generated.
landmarks.$reachable: A landmark you cannot walk to is scenery. Breadth-first over the walkable mask from the route's start, 4 m cells; every landmark must be reached and the path must not be absurdly longer than the straight line.
landmarks.$minUnique: Each landmark must be structurally unlike the generator's output. Measured as: no landmark's footprint-and-height signature may be reproducible by the building generator's own parameter ranges.
